name: Radionics

lead: Radionics is an early-20th-century practice built around boxes with dials and wiring that practitioners say can detect and correct 'frequencies' associated with health and illness. It began with the San Francisco physician Albert Abrams around 1909 and later spread through figures such as Ruth Drown and George de la Warr.

People who follow it describe the goal as restoring balance and vitality, and looksmaxxing-adjacent discussions treat that as a route to better skin, energy and overall appearance. Published reviews and regulators describe no demonstrated diagnostic or therapeutic effect, and several radionic makers faced legal action.

paras: Traditionally a practitioner takes a 'witness', such as a blood spot, hair sample, photograph or signature, and tunes dials on a device to numeric 'rates' linked to a condition. The 'treatment' is then broadcast, sometimes at a distance. Modern versions include computerised units and apps.

The main documented concern is that people may rely on a device in place of conventional medical care; the American Cancer Society warns about this for electromagnetic treatments. The US FDA does not recognise a medical use for radionic devices, a 1951 US court convicted Ruth Drown of misbranding, and the VIBE machine had a Class I recall in 2008.

chain: Practitioner 'tunes' a dial device to a rate linked to a condition
Broadcast of the 'remedy rate' is said to rebalance body energy
Better health and vitality claimed, which proponents associate with a healthier look
angle.text: Followers describe radionics as a way to restore energy balance, and some connect that to clearer skin, vitality and a healthier appearance. The effect is a claim made by practitioners; no published trial has measured appearance outcomes.

lead: Radionics, also called the Abrams method or electromagnetic therapy, is an alternative-medicine practice in which a device with dials is said to detect and correct disturbances in the body's 'energy frequencies'. [1] Practitioners and users generally describe the aim as restoring balance and vitality; in appearance-focused communities this is sometimes framed as supporting skin, energy and general wellbeing, which would show in how a person looks. These appearance claims are indirect and are a claimed effect rather than a documented one.

The practice dates to the work of the American physician Albert Abrams, who published books on diagnosis in 1909 and 1910 and later described a system he called Electronic Reactions of Abrams. [1][2] He leased his devices to physicians and, according to Wikipedia, became wealthy doing so; the American Medical Association called him the 'dean of gadget quacks'. [1] Later practitioners included Ruth Drown in the United States and George de la Warr in Britain. [2]

Mainstream science regards radionics as pseudoscience, saying it lacks a proposed mechanism consistent with physics and biology, and no radionic device has been shown to diagnose or treat disease. [1] A 1924 Scientific American investigation concluded that Abrams's method was 'at best' an illusion. [1] The term also turns up in unrelated medical literature, where 'Radionics' is a manufacturer of radiofrequency surgical and radiosurgery equipment, and 'radiomics' refers to image analysis; these are separate from the dial devices described here. [3][4]

paras: Radionic instruments are typically boxes with dials, knobs and wiring, sometimes with a rubber pad on which the practitioner strokes with a finger to judge a 'reaction'. Wikipedia notes that early devices were often simple and did not form a working electrical circuit, and that some modern practitioners describe them as focusing aids rather than functional machines. [1]

Practice centres on a 'witness', a blood spot, hair, photograph or signature that stands in for the patient. The practitioner sets dials to numerical 'rates' associated with conditions and then 'broadcasts' a corrective rate, including at a distance. Applications are also claimed for animals, plants and soil, and some practitioners blend in homeopathy or dowsing. [2]

Albert Abrams published Spinal Therapeutics (1909) and Spondylotherapy (1910), and in 1916 New Concepts in Diagnosis and Treatment, presenting his system as Electronic Reactions of Abrams. [1] He leased thirteen devices to practitioners, including the Oscilloclast intended for treatment. [1][2] He died in 1924, the year a Scientific American investigation examined his devices. [1]

Ruth Drown extended the approach to remote diagnosis from photographs in the 1930s, George de la Warr built dial instruments in Britain and helped found the Radionic Association in 1943, and T. Galen Hieronymus received a US patent in 1949, according to Grokipedia. [2] Contemporary versions include computerised units and software. [1][2]

Wikipedia reports that radionic claims conflict with established physics and biology, that no mechanism has been demonstrated, and that no radionic device has been shown to diagnose or treat any condition. [1] The American Cancer Society warns that relying on electromagnetic devices alone and avoiding conventional care may have serious consequences. [1]

Broader reviews of electromagnetic therapies, which are a different category from radionics, have examined pulsed fields for pain, ulcers and fractures and generally reported insufficient or no benefit versus control. [1]

According to Grokipedia, a US federal court convicted Ruth Drown of misbranding in 1951, and authorities later banned devices such as her Homoe-Vibra Ray. [2] The FDA does not recognise any legitimate medical use for radionic devices, and the VIBE machine from Vibe Technologies received a Class I recall in 2008. [1]

No studies found. Grokipedia mentions small trials from the 1990s and 2000s of radionically prepared remedies that found results no better than placebo, though it does not identify them in detail. [2] Medical papers that mention 'radionics' generally refer to the equipment manufacturer or to radiomics image analysis, not to dial devices. [3][4][5]

Radionics is a peripheral topic in appearance communities. It appears alongside other energy-device claims, where it is presented as a route to wellbeing that proponents say shows in skin and general condition.

lore.intro: Followers describe radionics as a form of subtle-energy therapy for wellbeing; appearance claims are secondary and indirect. [1]
